body:
This PR was implemented by Claude Code. I did not review the code, hence marking it as draft for now. The final summary imlementation of the Claude is below.

Fixes #7566 

## Motivation

Indexing a memoryview argument generates `((double *) __pyx_v_y.data) + i`. The C compiler
can't tell that the data of two memoryviews never overlaps. So it adds a runtime overlap
check and a scalar fallback loop, or it skips optimizations entirely.

The C `restrict` qualifier removes that uncertainty. GCC 14 only honours `restrict` on
**function parameters**, not on local variables  [1][2][3]. A `restrict` local copied from `.data` had
no effect in any test.

[1] https://discourse.llvm.org/t/rfc-yet-another-llvm-restrict-support/87612?utm_source=chatgpt.com
[2] https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=120972
[3] https://gcc.gnu.org/pipermail/gcc-bugs/2025-July/920752.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com

## Syntax

```cython
cdef void saxpy(const double[::1] restrict x, double[::1] restrict y, double a) noexcept nogil:
    for i in range(y.shape[0]):
        y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]

def f(double[:, :] restrict m):   # def functions are supported too
    ...
```

- `restrict` goes between the type and the argument name.
- `restrict` can still be used as an argument name: `def f(int restrict)`.
- `T restrict name` also works for pointer typedefs. For any other type (`int`, `object`, …)
  it is a compile error.

## Generated code

For a function with `restrict` memoryview arguments, Cython generates two C functions:

```c
/* body: force-inlined, data pointers passed as restrict parameters */
static CYTHON_FORCE_INLINE void __pyx_ri_f_..._saxpy(
        __Pyx_memviewslice __pyx_v_x, __Pyx_memviewslice __pyx_v_y, double __pyx_v_a,
        char *CYTHON_RESTRICT __pyx_dp_v_x, char *CYTHON_RESTRICT __pyx_dp_v_y) {
    ... original body; element access uses __pyx_dp_v_x / __pyx_dp_v_y ...
}

/* wrapper: original name and signature */
static void __pyx_f_..._saxpy(__Pyx_memviewslice __pyx_v_x, __Pyx_memviewslice __pyx_v_y, double __pyx_v_a) {
    __pyx_ri_f_..._saxpy(__pyx_v_x, __pyx_v_y, __pyx_v_a, __pyx_v_x.data, __pyx_v_y.data);
}
```

- **Wrapper:** keeps the original name and signature, so callers, `.pxd` declarations,
  vtables and function pointers are unchanged.
- **`CYTHON_FORCE_INLINE`** is a new macro. It expands to `__attribute__((always_inline))` on
  GCC/Clang and `__forceinline` on MSVC.
- **Slices:** slices of a `restrict` argument are taken from its `restrict` pointer.
- **Non-`restrict` memoryview arguments** get a plain local copy of the data pointer. Its
  declaration is only emitted if the copy is used.
- **Excluded arguments:** arguments that are reassigned in the body or captured by a closure
  get no pointer copy and no `restrict` parameter.

## Benefits

GCC 14, `-O3 -march=native`. Each case compares a plain memoryview function with one that
uses `restrict` memoryview arguments.

| Optimization | Example | Plain | `restrict` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overlap check removed | `y[i] = a*x[i] + y[i]*y[i]` | check + scalar fallback loop | vector loop only |
| Load moved out of the loop | `y[i] += x[0]` | 68 instructions, reloads `x[0]` | 43 instructions, loaded once |
| Accumulate in a register | `s[0] += a[i]` | load + store every iteration | register, unrolled 4×, one store |
| Skip a reload after a store | `a[0]=1; b[0]=2; return a[0]` | reloads `a[0]` | constant `1.0` |
| Vectorize indirect indexing | `y[i] = 2*x[idx[i]]` | not vectorized | vectorized |
| Vectorize code without a loop | `a[0..3] = b[0..3]*2` | 4 scalar operations | one 256-bit operation |

Runtime (best of 5):

| Kernel | n | Plain | `restrict` memoryview | `restrict` pointers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| saxpy | 4 | 5.2 ns | 5.2 ns | 5.1 ns |
| saxpy | 10 000 | 1596 ns | 1612 ns | 1626 ns |
| indirect indexing | 64 | 19.5 ns | **15.5 ns** | – |
| indirect indexing | 10 000 | 5263 ns | **5093 ns** | – |

The saxpy kernel shows no gain because its overlap check is cheap. The gains appear where
GCC can't build an overlap check at all: indirect indexing, code without a loop, and loops
that use many pointers.

## Overhead

- **Inlining:** no `__pyx_ri_*` function was left as a separate function at `-O0`, `-O1`,
  `-O2`, `-O3` or `-Os`, so it was inlined into its wrapper every time.
- **Machine code:** compared on pairs where `restrict` can't help (one memoryview, read-only
  access, Python objects with exceptions, `*args`/`**kwargs`). Alignment padding and the
  source line numbers in error handling were ignored.

  | Level | Result |
  |---|---|
  | `-O2`, `-O3` | identical |
  | `-O1` | same instructions, registers swapped |
  | `-Os` | `restrict` version 2 instructions shorter |
  | `-O0` | `restrict` version +17 to +33 instructions (extra parameter copies kept) |

- **Calls:** no measurable call overhead (5.2 ns in both versions at n=4).
- **Warnings and C++:** no new warnings with `-Wall -Wextra`, and the code compiles as C++.

## Limitations

- **User promise:** `restrict` is a promise from the user. If the memory behind a `restrict`
  argument is also changed through another memoryview or pointer during the call, the
  behaviour is undefined, as in C.
- **Pure-Python syntax:** no `cython.restrict[...]` annotation support yet.
- **No body split:** C++ class methods, templates and varargs functions fall back to a local
  `restrict` copy, which GCC ignores.
- **`-O0`:** debug builds are slightly larger. A check on `__OPTIMIZE__` could skip the split
  there.
- **Compilers:** only tested with GCC 14. Clang and MSVC are untested.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `Cython/Compiler/Parsing.py` | parse `T restrict name` |
| `Cython/Compiler/Nodes.py` | handle `restrict` on memoryview arguments; carry the flag to argument entries; generate the force-inlined body and wrapper (`FuncDefNode`, `CFuncDefNode`, `DefNode`) |
| `Cython/Compiler/PyrexTypes.py` | `CFuncTypeArg.is_restrict` (kept for fused types); memoryview lookups use the data pointer copy |
| `Cython/Compiler/MemoryView.py` | element access and slicing use the data pointer copy |
| `Cython/Compiler/Symtab.py` | new `Entry` attributes `memview_data_cname`, `memview_data_used`, `memview_restrict` |
| `Cython/Compiler/Naming.py` | prefixes `__pyx_dp_` (data pointer) and `__pyx_ri_` (body function) |
| `Cython/Utility/ModuleSetupCode.c` | `CYTHON_FORCE_INLINE` macro |

## Tests

- **`tests/run/memview_restrict.pyx`** (new): cdef/def/cpdef functions, strided 2D, recursion,
  reassigned arguments, closures, slicing, optional arguments, fused types, cdef class
  methods, `None` defaults, `*args`/`**kwargs`, `restrict` as a name. It also checks the
  generated C.
- **`tests/errors/memview_restrict_errors.pyx`** (new): `int restrict` and `object restrict`
  are errors; a `restrict` pointer typedef is accepted.
- **Regression:** 2,673 existing tests passed in C and C++, covering memoryview, buffer,
  fused, qualifier, cpdef, closure, def-argument and pure-mode tests.

comment_data.body: Now thinking, using force inline can be a problem for more exotic C compilers where it can introduce performance degradation when the "restrict function" is not inlined (`inline` keyword is used but the compiler for some reason ignores it)...
comment_data.diff_hunk:
@@ -503,6 +503,17 @@
   #endif
 #endif
 
+// forced inlining (used for the body of functions with restrict memoryview arguments)
+#ifndef CYTHON_FORCE_INLINE

comment_data.body:
It seems that ICC supports `__forceinline` too:
```suggestion
  #elif defined(_MSC_VER) || defined(__INTEL_COMPILER)
```
comment_data.diff_hunk:
@@ -503,6 +503,17 @@
   #endif
 #endif
 
+// forced inlining (used for the body of functions with restrict memoryview arguments)
+#ifndef CYTHON_FORCE_INLINE
+  #if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
+    #define CYTHON_FORCE_INLINE CYTHON_INLINE __attribute__((__always_inline__))
+  #elif defined(_MSC_VER)
